title: Same solver, same mesh, 60% apart
subtitle: Hypersonic flow over a spiked blunt body · 2D axisymmetric RANS in Ansys Fluent, validated against Huebner and Roveda (2009)
thesis: At Mach 6 the turbulence model, not the mesh or the solver, decided whether the simulation matched the experiment — and residuals alone couldn't tell a good solution from a broken one.
tldr: Reproduced a classic Mach 6.06 benchmark — a spiked hemisphere-cylinder — with 2D axisymmetric RANS in Ansys Fluent, across 14 production runs on an HPC cluster.
SST k-ω and Spalart–Allmaras land within 5.5% and 4.3% mean error of the experiment, level with the best code in the original paper and closing the ~35% gap it reported for Fluent.
Changing only the turbulence model moved dome pressure by ~60% and drag by ~50%. The mesh moved it by under 8%; inlet turbulence by under 1%.
The cause is physical: k-ε keeps the spike's boundary layer attached ~75 mm too long, shrinking the recirculating bubble that shields the nose.
Three runs passed their residual targets but still held non-physical cells above 1000 K, and one configuration diverged on both meshes — residuals alone are not an acceptance test at Mach 6.
It ends with the ten-point checklist I now run before trusting any hypersonic RANS result.

body:
At Mach 6 a blunt nose makes a strong, detached bow shock. Behind it the pressure, the heating and the drag are all brutal. One old trick is to stick a thin spike out in front of the nose with a small disc on the end — an *aerodisk*. The spike pushes the shock system forward, swaps the one strong shock for a set of weaker oblique ones, and wraps the nose in a pocket of slow, recirculating air that shields it.

That pocket is exactly what makes it hard to simulate. The flow separates, forms a shear layer, reattaches on the nose with its own shock, and all of it is decided by turbulence. I wanted to know how much of the answer comes from the physics and how much from the settings I pick, so before using CFD to design anything I tried to reproduce a known result.

```keynumbers
M∞ 6.06 | Freestream Mach number | p∞ = 1951 Pa, T∞ = 58.25 K
2.1 × 10⁶ | Reynolds number | based on dome diameter
14 | Production runs | + 1 exploratory, 128 cores each
4 | Turbulence models compared | SST k-ω, SA, standard and realizable k-ε
```

## The benchmark

The reference is Roveda's 2009 AIAA benchmark of three commercial codes (CFD++, Cobalt and Fluent) on spiked blunt bodies, which compares them against two sets of experiments. I took *Model 1*: Huebner's spiked hemisphere-cylinder at Mach 6.06 and zero incidence, with eight measured surface pressures on the dome.

The paper's conclusions are what made it worth repeating. CFD++ matched the experiment well. Cobalt and Fluent under-predicted the dome pressure badly. The authors put most of the spread down to turbulence modelling and the location of separation along the spike. That is a claim you can test.

```figure /case-studies/aerospike/geometry.webp
Model 1 geometry, measured from the aerodisk face. Aerodisk Ø29.36 mm, sting Ø9.53 mm, hemispherical dome Ø76.2 mm, body Ø101.6 mm; 305.1 mm from the aerodisk face to the dome apex. Every dimension matches the paper's Table 1.
```

So the question was simple: **can a 2D axisymmetric Fluent model reproduce Model 1, and do the paper's explanations hold up?**

## Setting it up

The geometry is axisymmetric at zero incidence, so I modelled a 2D wedge about the body axis. That made it cheap enough to run every combination I wanted, instead of picking one and hoping.

| Boundary | Type | Settings |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outer curved boundary | Pressure far-field | M∞ = 6.06, p∞ = 1951 Pa, T∞ = 58.25 K, inlet turbulence per case |
| Downstream | Pressure outlet | p = 1951 Pa, T = 58.25 K for backflow |
| y = 0 | Axis | 2D axisymmetric about x |
| Aerodisk, sting, dome, body | Wall | No-slip, adiabatic |

```figure /case-studies/aerospike/domain_bc.webp
The 2D axisymmetric domain and boundary conditions, with the body walls in the inset.
```

```deepdive Solver settings, in full
| Setting | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Solver | Density-based, implicit, steady, 2D axisymmetric (Fluent 2025 R2, double precision) |
| Flux / gradients | AUSM flux; Green-Gauss node-based gradients; second-order upwind |
| Gas | Air as an ideal gas, Sutherland viscosity |
| Courant number | 5, operating pressure 0 Pa |
| Initialisation | Hybrid initialisation |
| Convergence | Scaled residuals 10⁻⁶ (10⁻⁵ with AMR) **plus** a dome-pressure monitor, up to 30,000 iterations |
| Compute | Batch runs from Fluent journal files on an HPC cluster, 128 cores per job |

Each case starts from the same base case file read fresh, so no run inherits a flow field from another. That matters more than it sounds: when you sweep models in one session, it is easy for the "SA" run to quietly still be running the previous model.

**Inlet turbulence.** The paper ran CFD++ at three freestream turbulence levels, so I used the same three:

| Config | Turbulence intensity | Viscosity ratio μt/μ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| S20 | 5% | 10 |
| S21 | 2% | 50 |
| S22 | 2% | 150 |
```

## The mesh: getting y+ under 1

The dome pressure depends on where the boundary layer on the sting separates, and separation is a near-wall event. So the near-wall resolution wasn't a nice-to-have — it was the point.

I built a quad-dominant mesh with 15 inflation layers on every wall and ran four meshes from 31k to 188k cells. Going from Mesh 3 (103,535 cells) to Mesh 4 changed the drag by **1.4%** for 83% more cells, so Mesh 3 became the baseline for everything.

```figure /case-studies/aerospike/mesh_zoom.webp
Mesh 3 close up: the aerodisk, the sting–dome junction and the inflation layers at the dome shoulder.
```

```figure /case-studies/aerospike/yplus.webp
First-cell y+ along every wall. Median 0.30, 95th percentile 0.68 — the viscous sub-layer is resolved, as SST k-ω and Spalart–Allmaras need. The one spike (y+ ≈ 4.8) is the aerodisk's front corner; adaptive refinement brings it down to 1.3.
```

```caution This mesh is wrong for k-ε, on purpose
Standard k-ε is calibrated for wall functions, around y+ ≳ 30. At y+ < 1 it is running outside the range it was built for. I kept one mesh for every model so the comparison stays fair — but it is part of why k-ε does badly below, and it is worth knowing before blaming the model alone.
```

```deepdive Mesh quality numbers
| Metric | Mesh 3 | AMR mesh (SST k-ω, S20) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cells (quad / tri / polygon) | 103,535 (102,399 / 1,136 / 0) | 327,497 (308,526 / 555 / 18,416) |
| Orthogonal quality, min / mean | 0.239 / 0.988 | 0.064 / 0.948 |
| Cells with orthogonal quality < 0.5 | 0.04% | 3.8% |
| Aspect ratio, max / mean | 20.4 / 2.59 | 38.2 / 2.55 |

The low minima on the AMR mesh are hanging-node cells where refinement levels meet — expected, and away from the walls.

| Mesh | Cells | Aerodisk size (mm) | Global size (mm) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 31k | 1.50 | 1 – 15 |
| 2 | 65k | 1.00 | 0.75 – 15 |
| 3 | 103k | 0.50 | 0.5 – 10 |
| 4 | 188k | 0.25 | 0.25 – 5 |
```

## What the flow looks like

```figure /case-studies/aerospike/mach_annotated.webp
Mach number, SST k-ω. A bow shock off the aerodisk, a separated shear layer enclosing a slow recirculation zone over the sting, a reattachment shock on the dome shoulder, then an expansion fan around the body.
```

The spike does what it's supposed to. Instead of one strong bow shock on the nose, there is a weak shock off the disc and a conical shear layer that encloses the slow air in front of the dome. Where that shear layer lands on the dome shoulder, it makes the reattachment shock — and the highest pressure on the nose. Everything below comes back to where that landing happens.

## The headline result: dome pressure

This is the plot that matters. Toggle the curves, switch between the fixed mesh and AMR, and hover to read values.

```chart domePressure
Dome surface pressure against arc length from the dome apex. Benchmark curves are digitised from Roveda (2009), Fig. 12, and replotted.
```

SST k-ω and Spalart–Allmaras sit on the experimental points and on top of the CFD++ curves — the code the paper rated best. The Fluent result in the paper sits about 35% low. Standard k-ε goes the other way entirely: a hump mid-dome and a shoulder peak near P/P∞ ≈ 10.8, double the experiment.

```chart errorMetrics
Error at the eight Huebner points, by linear interpolation of each curve. The CFD++ and paper-Fluent rows use the same digitised data.
```

```finding The Fluent gap in the paper is a setup issue, not the code
With SST k-ω or SA and a wall-resolved mesh, Fluent lands within 5.5% and 4.3% mean error of the experiment — in line with CFD++ (3.8%) and nowhere near the ~35% under-prediction reported for Fluent. Same solver, different settings, different answer.
```

The single biggest error sits at s ≈ 0.77 in, where the experiment has a local bump that no RANS model I ran reproduces. I'd rather say that than smooth it over.

## Why k-ε gets it so wrong

A 60% error isn't noise, so it's worth chasing down. The streamlines show it straight away.

```figure /case-studies/aerospike/streamlines.webp
Streamlines and Mach number in the recirculation zone. SST k-ω and SA: the bubble runs from x ≈ 0.18 m all the way to the dome. Standard k-ε: the bubble shrinks to x ≈ 0.26–0.30 m and the fast shear layer hits close to the dome apex.
```

```figure /case-studies/aerospike/sting_cf.webp
Skin friction (top) and pressure (bottom) along the sting. Cf changes sign where the boundary layer separates: x = 0.182 m for SST, 0.192 m for SA, and 0.258 m for k-ε — about 75 mm later.
```

Here's the chain. k-ε has no limiter on turbulence production, so it piles turbulent energy into the sting boundary layer. A more turbulent boundary layer resists the adverse pressure gradient for longer, so it separates ~75 mm later. A later separation means a smaller bubble. A smaller bubble shields less of the dome, so the shear layer lands near the apex — **+60% dome pressure and +50% drag (193 N vs 129 N)**.

```figure /case-studies/aerospike/models_pratio.webp
P/P∞ fields for SST k-ω, Spalart–Allmaras and standard k-ε. With k-ε the recompression collapses into one strong shock on the dome instead of a long weak oblique one.
```

I also tried realizable k-ε, expecting it to do better. It was worse: peak P/P∞ ≈ 13 and 110% mean error. Both k-ε variants make the same mistake about separation, and that is the mistake that matters here.

```finding Separation along the sting controls the nose
The paper's explanation holds: change where the sting boundary layer separates and you change the bubble, the reattachment point, the dome pressure and the drag. The turbulence model decides where it separates.
```

## Temperature barely cares

```chart domeTemperature
Dome surface temperature. Benchmark points digitised by eye from Roveda (2009), Fig. 13, so treat them as approximate (about ±0.05 in T/T∞).
```

Pressure swings by 60% between models. Temperature moves by about 2%. Every model gives T/T∞ ≈ 8.0–8.2, close to CFD++ and Cobalt, and just under the adiabatic recovery limit of 8.34. That's what you'd expect with an adiabatic wall: the slow air in the bubble recovers nearly to stagnation temperature, whatever the turbulence model.

The paper's Fluent result, at 5–6, is about 30% below every other code. The paper doesn't say what wall thermal condition that run used. If it wasn't adiabatic, that alone could explain the gap — one more setting quietly deciding an answer.

## A setting that didn't matter: inlet turbulence

In the paper, changing the freestream turbulence moved the CFD++ dome pressure by 5–7%. In my runs, S20, S21 and S22 collapse onto each other: under 1% for SST, under 3% for k-ε.

```figure /case-studies/aerospike/mut_ratio.webp
Turbulent viscosity ratio for SST and k-ε at S20 and S21. The freestream value has almost vanished by the time the flow reaches the aerodisk; the shear layer generates its own, with μt/μ of 100–1000.
```

The inlet values were applied correctly — ahead of the body μt/μ is about 5 for S20 and 35 for S21. But freestream turbulence decays by roughly two orders of magnitude between the far field and the aerodisk, and the separated shear layer makes far more of its own. By the time it matters, the inlet setting has been forgotten.

```figure /case-studies/aerospike/turb_decay.webp
Turbulent kinetic energy and viscosity ratio along a line from the far field to the body: the freestream turbulence decays long before it reaches anything that matters.
```

## AMR: sharper shocks, same answer

Adaptive mesh refinement on a density-gradient shock sensor tripled the cell count (103,535 → 327,497), concentrated on the bow shock, the shear layer and the reattachment shock. Drag the slider to compare.

```chart schlierenCompare
Numerical schlieren, exp(−k|∇ρ|/|∇ρ|max), on the fixed mesh and after adaptation. The shocks get much thinner; they don't move.
```

The shocks went from smeared to crisp, but drag changed by under 1% and the aft-dome pressure by 3–8%. The stagnation pressure behind the disc moved from 51.3 to 49.3 P∞ — closer to the 47.8 that normal-shock theory gives. So AMR made the solution better looking and slightly more correct, without changing any conclusion.

```chart sensitivity
How much each choice moved the result, from the runs above. The turbulence model dominates by more than ten times.
```

## When "converged" isn't converged

This is the part I'd want someone to tell me before my first hypersonic run.

```chart runMatrix
The full production matrix. Green met every criterion; amber met the residual target but failed another check; red diverged.
```

- **Standard k-ε at S20 diverged on both meshes.** Temperature climbed to Fluent's 5000 K clamp across the wake and up to the dome shoulder. I left it out of every comparison, which is why k-ε results use S21 and S22.
- **SA S20 and SST S20 on AMR converged — and were still wrong somewhere.** Residuals dropped below target, drag settled, and yet a pocket of cells behind the base corner sat above 1000 K. The physical maximum here is the stagnation temperature, 486 K. The forebody and the drag were unaffected, so those results stand, but nothing in the residual plot would have told me.
- **Some runs stopped on the residual criterion while the dome-pressure monitor was still drifting by 1–2%.**

```figure /case-studies/aerospike/wake_anomaly.webp
Static temperature behind the body. Left: the diverged k-ε S20 run, with 5000 K across the wake. Right: the SA S20 run, with a much smaller non-physical pocket confined to the base corner.
```

```figure /case-studies/aerospike/monitors.webp
Area-averaged dome pressure through each run. SST and SA settle at P/P∞ ≈ 4.1 on Mesh 3 and 4.3–4.5 with AMR; k-ε at ≈ 6.9–7.2. The long transients come from the reattachment point travelling along the dome before it locks in.
```

```caution Residuals are not an acceptance test
At Mach 6, a run can pass every residual target and still contain physically impossible cells. Before I accept a hypersonic solution now, I check that the peak temperature is below T₀, that the force monitor and a surface-pressure monitor have flattened, and that integrated loads add up.
```

That last one is cheap and catches a lot. Integrating wall pressure (126.9 N) and wall shear (≈1.6 N) by hand gives 128.5 N, against the 128.6 N Fluent reports. When those two numbers disagree, something in the post-processing or the solution is off.

## The checklist I use now

Everything above boils down to a list. None of it is exotic, which is the point: each item is a default you can leave untouched, and each one changed or protected the answer here.

1. **Validate before you design.** Reproduce a known case at the same Mach number first. Without Model 1, I'd have had no way to know that a 60% error was an error.
2. **Pick the turbulence model for the physics, then justify it.** For separated, shock-dominated hypersonic flow, SST k-ω was the robust choice here. The model was the single biggest lever in the whole study.
3. **Match the mesh to the model.** y+ < 1 for SST and SA; wall functions and y+ ≈ 30+ if you insist on k-ε. Don't judge a model on a mesh it wasn't built for.
4. **Resolve the walls where separation happens.** Inflation layers on every wall, refined at the corners. Separation location drove every result.
5. **Use a shock-capturing flux and second-order schemes.** Density-based with AUSM, and AMR on a density-gradient sensor if you can afford it — it sharpened shocks without moving them.
6. **Decide your wall thermal condition deliberately.** It controls the surface temperature far more than the turbulence model does. Write it down — the paper's Fluent run didn't, and it is the odd one out.
7. **Check where your inlet turbulence ends up.** Freestream values decay fast. If a result depends on them, look at what actually reaches the body.
8. **Don't trust residuals alone.** Monitor a surface quantity and the forces, and check T_max ≤ T₀. Three of my "converged" runs had non-physical cells.
9. **Start every case clean.** Read a fresh case for each run, so one model never inherits another's flow field or settings.
10. **Close the loop on loads.** Integrate pressure and shear yourself and compare with the solver's force report.

## Limits, and what's next

- **One geometry, one condition.** Only Model 1 at zero incidence. The paper's Model 2 (Mach 4.5, 16° incidence) needs a 3D model and I haven't attempted it yet.
- **Steady RANS.** Spiked-body shear layers can oscillate and pulse. A steady solution can't show that.
- **Digitised benchmark data.** The comparison curves are digitised from the paper's figures, the temperature ones by eye.
- **Not every model at every inlet level.** SA and realizable k-ε were only run at S20.
- **No formal uncertainty.** Grid independence rests on the four-mesh drag study; there's no Richardson extrapolation or GCI.

Next up is a 3D cross-check in OpenFOAM with the density-based `rhoCentralFoam` solver, which is set up on the cluster for SST k-ω and k-ε. After that: unsteady runs to look for shear-layer oscillation, isothermal walls to get actual heat flux on the dome, and then a proper design sweep of spike length, disc size and incidence. I'll add the OpenFOAM results here when they're in.
